hypotheses.statement: There is an infinite finitely presented unital associative algebra $$R=\bigoplus_{d\geq0}R_d=\mathbb F_2\oplus I, \qquad R_0=\mathbb F_2, \qquad I=\bigoplus_{d\geq1}R_d,$$ such that every $R_d$ is finite-dimensional and $I$ is matrix-nil. This algebra has the word presentation and hierarchy specified in Proposition 3.

The algebra $R$ in Proposition 2 is the first algebra $A_0$ of a sequence $(A_j)_{j\geq0}$ with the following properties. There are positive integers $c,k,h_0,D$, with $D>10(c+1)(k+1)$, and $$h_j=h_0D^j,\qquad L_j=2\cdot2^{h_j}+1.$$ For each $j\geq0$:* 1. *$A_j$ is presented by a finite alphabet $\Sigma_j$, finitely many replacements, and finitely many zero declarations, all of length at most $k$. It is graded by word length.* 2. *There is a substitution $E_j$ sending each letter of $\Sigma_{j+1}$ to a word of length $L_j$ over $\Sigma_j$. Extended by concatenation, it induces a unital algebra homomorphism $A_{j+1}\to A_j$.* 3. *A specified subset of $\Sigma_j$ gives cuts immediately before its letters. There are integers $B_j,T_j\geq0$ and a finite set of words $\mathcal T_j$ such that every nonzero word $w$ of length at least $T_j$ has the unique decomposition $$\label{eq:token-decomposition} w=p_w\,t_1\cdots t_r\,s_w, \qquad |p_w|,|s_w|\leq B_j,\qquad t_i\in\mathcal T_j.$$ Here $p_w$ precedes the first cut, $s_w$ begins at the last cut, and the $t_i$ are exactly the intervals between consecutive cuts. A cut is counted only if its following letter occurs in the word. For each $t\in\mathcal T_j$ there is a nonempty word $u_t$ over $\Sigma_{j+1}$ such that $$\label{eq:token-upper-word} 1\leq |u_t|\leq k,\qquad |t|=L_j|u_t|,\qquad [t]=[E_j(u_t)]\quad\hbox{in }A_j.$$

For every integer $d\geq0$, put $$L=L_0L_1\cdots L_d.$$ There is an integer $N\geq1$ such that every nonzero word $w$ in $R$ of length at least $N$ has a start phase $\sigma(w)\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$ and an end phase $$\tau(w)=\sigma(w)+|w|\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$$ with the following properties:*

1.  *Both phases depend only on the basis class of $w$.*


2.  *If $v$ is a contiguous subword of $w$, has length at least $N$, and starts at offset $b$ from the beginning of $w$, then $$\label{eq:phase-subword}
     \sigma(v)=\sigma(w)+b.$$*

*The integers $L$ so obtained are odd and arbitrarily large.

Fix $L,N,\sigma,\tau$ from Lemma 4. If $u,v$ are nonzero basis words of lengths at least $N$, then $$\tau(u)\ne\sigma(v)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad uv=0.$$ If $uv\ne0$, its phases satisfy $\sigma(uv)=\sigma(u)$ and $\tau(uv)=\tau(v)$.

Let $S,T$ be disjoint finite sets of coordinates. The subgroup generated by $x_{ij}(a)$ with $i\in S$, $j\in T$ maps isomorphically onto the additive group of matrices supported in $S\times T$ under $u\mapsto
\pi(u)-I$. A word supported on $S$ normalizes this subgroup and acts on its entries by left multiplication by its matrix on $S$. On the reverse strip $T\times S$, its action is right multiplication by the inverse matrix on $S$.
For every $B$, the group $J(B)$ is central in $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(B)$.

In characteristic two, every permutation of a finite set of coordinates is induced on roots by conjugation in the Steinberg group after adjoining an outside coordinate if necessary. In particular, relabeling the finitely many coordinates in a representative of $z\in J(B)$ leaves the element $z$ unchanged in $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(B)$.
In any group, let $A=[X,Y]$ and $B'=[Y,Z]$. If $$[X,Z]=[A,X]=[B',Z]=[A,B']=1,$$ then $[A,Z]=[X,B']$. This common commutator commutes with $A,Z,X,B'$.

The block roots satisfy the Steinberg relations over $\mathop{\mathrm{Mat}}_b(B)$: $$\begin{aligned}
 X_{ij}(A+A')&=X_{ij}(A)X_{ij}(A'),\\
 [X_{ij}(A),X_{kl}(A')]&=1
       &&\text{if }j\ne k\text{ and }i\ne l,\\
 [X_{ij}(A),X_{jk}(A')]&=X_{ik}(AA')
       &&\text{if }i,j,k\text{ are distinct}.
\end{aligned}$$ Consequently they define a homomorphism $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_n(\mathop{\mathrm{Mat}}_b(B))\longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_{nb}(B)$. Moreover, for every $P\in\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_b(\mathbb F_2)$ there is an element $q\in\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_{nb}(B)$ such that $$q^{-1}X_{ij}(A)q=X_{ij}(P^{-1}AP)
 \qquad(i\ne j).$$ Its matrix image is the block diagonal matrix with a copy of $P$ in every outer block.

Let $U$ be generated by the roots $x_{(i,s),(j,t)}(a)$ with $s<t$, allowing $i=j$. Then $U$ injects into its matrix image and is normalized by every root whose inner indices agree. If a root word $v(t)$ over $B[t]$ has identity matrix image, and $T\in\mathop{\mathrm{Mat}}_b(\mathbb F_2)$ is upper triangular with constant diagonal entry $\lambda$, then $$\label{eq:triangular-evaluation}
 W_v(T)=\prod_{s=0}^{b-1}\iota_s\bigl(v(\lambda)\bigr).$$

Let $v(t)$ be a product of $m\geq1$ root factors over $B[t]$, whose polynomial entries have degrees at most $d\geq0$. Suppose its matrix image is the identity over $B[t]$. Put $\delta=\max\{1,d\}$. If $$b>2(m+1)\delta,$$ then $W_v(C_b)=W_v(S_b)$ in $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_{nb}(B)$.

If $z\in J(R)$ maps to $1$ in $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(\mathbb F_2)$, then $$W_z(C_b)=1
 \qquad\text{for every sufficiently large integer }b.$$ More precisely, if the graded word $z(t)$ has $m\geq1$ factors of degrees at most $d$, it suffices that $b>2(m+1)\max\{1,d\}$.
Every element of $$J(R)\cap\ker\bigl(\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(R)\longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(\mathbb F_2)\bigr)$$ has finite $2$-power order.

For each coordinate $i$ and every nonzero word class $w$ satisfying $|w|\ge M$ and $\sigma(w)\ne\tau(w)$, there is an element $H_i(w)\in\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(R)$ with the following property. If $p,q$ are nonzero words with $$|p|,|q|\ge N,\qquad |p|+|q|\ge M,
 \qquad \sigma(p)\ne\tau(q),$$ then, for every $j\ne i$, $$\label{eq:long-opposite}
 [x_{ij}(p),x_{ji}(q)]
 =\begin{cases}
    H_i(w),& pq\text{ represents the nonzero class }w,\\
    1,& pq=0\text{ in }R.
   \end{cases}$$ The element $H_i(w)$ has square $1$ and matrix image $I+wE_{ii}$.
The subgroup $U(S,P)$ is abelian of exponent at most $2$, and the matrix map is injective on it. Every root with a consistent entry normalizes $U(S,P)$.

Suppose $z\in J(R)$ is represented by a finite word $$\label{eq:high-word}
 z=\prod_{
u=1}^m x_{i_

 \qquad |w_
u|\ge M,$$ where every $w_
u$ is a nonzero word class. Label new coordinates by $(i,s)$, with $s\in\mathbb Z/L$. In the stable group, $$\label{eq:relocation}
 z=\prod_{
u=1}^m
 x_{(i_
u,\sigma(w_

u,	au(w_
u))}(w_
u).$$
Under the hypotheses of Lemma 18, $$\label{eq:odd-power} W_z(C_L)=z^L.$$

For every integer $M\ge1$, each element of $$\ker\bigl(\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(R)\longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(R/R_{\ge2M})\bigr)$$ can be represented by a finite product of roots whose entries are nonzero word classes of lengths at least $M$.

For such an algebra $B$, the following statements hold.*

1.  *Every tuple of columns of $B^m$ with linearly independent reductions in $\mathbb F_2^m$ extends to an invertible matrix.*

2.  *The kernel $J_r(B)$ is central in $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_r(B)$ for $r\geq6$.*

3.  *For $r\geq5$, the group $\mathop{\mathrm{E}}_r(B)$ is normal in $\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_r(B)$, and the natural maps $$\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_r(B)/\mathop{\mathrm{E}}_r(B)\longrightarrow
     \mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_{r+1}(B)/\mathop{\mathrm{E}}_{r+1}(B)$$ are isomorphisms.

Let $B=\mathbb F_2\oplus I_B$ satisfy the hypotheses of Proposition 22. For every $n\geq12$, the standard stabilization map $J_n(B)\to J_{n+1}(B)$ is an isomorphism, and the natural homomorphism $$\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_n(B)\longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{St}}(B)$$ is injective.
The augmented chain complex $C_\bullet(m)$ is exact in degrees at most $m-2$.

For every $d\ge1$, the group $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_{12}(R/R_{\ge d})$ is finite. The homomorphisms $$\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_{12}(R)\longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_{12}(R/R_{\ge d}),\qquad d\ge1,$$ separate the elements of $\mathop{\mathrm{St}}_{12}(R)$.

coverage.checked_domain: Exhaustive sizes 1 through 12; power-of-two cases 1, 2, 4, 8 and all remaining sizes as controls.
coverage.oracle_basis: Exact binomial coefficients accumulated modulo 2 by residues, with every output entry rechecked independently of matrix exponentiation.
